lesson.title: Pupils’ data: collect less, protect more
lesson.subtitle: What counts as personal data, and how to keep it safe

video.title: Pupils’ data: collect less, protect more
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds; narration in the lesson language, captions as separate files.
cast: Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher (main character)
Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Staff room. Amina holds her phone over the parents’ group, a results sheet in her other hand. Her thumb stops above Send.
scenes.animation: Results sheet slides in; her thumb freezes; slow push-in on her face.
scenes.narration: The results are out, so I’ll just post the whole list in the parents’ group. Forty names, forty marks. Wait. Would I want my own child’s mark shown to thirty-nine other families?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the course name.
scenes.on_screen_text: Pupils’ data: collect less, protect more
scenes.narration: Today: pupils’ personal data — what it is, and how to collect less and protect more.

scenes.visual: Two columns: everyday personal data, then a red column of sensitive data.
scenes.animation: Items drop into each column as they are named.
scenes.narration: Personal data is anything that shows who a pupil is, or tells you something about them. A name, a photo, a phone number, an address. Marks and attendance too. Some data is sensitive: health, religion, a family’s money or problems. That needs the most care of all.

scenes.visual: Four cards with a scale icon: Kenya, Egypt, Nigeria, South Africa.
scenes.animation: Cards flip in as each country is named.
scenes.narration: Children can’t always speak up for themselves, so the law speaks up for them. Many countries now have a data protection law. Kenya has had one since twenty nineteen, Egypt since twenty twenty, and Nigeria since twenty twenty-three. South Africa has POPIA. The details differ, so check your own country’s law, but the big ideas are the same.

scenes.visual: A list of five big ideas, each with an icon.
scenes.animation: Rows appear as they are said.
scenes.narration: Here are the big ideas. Collect only what you need, for a clear reason. Keep it accurate. Keep it safe. Keep it only as long as you need it. And remember: parents and pupils have the right to see it and correct it.

scenes.visual: The school’s exam cupboard: one key on a hook, a padlock, a shredder.
scenes.animation: The cupboard door closes; the padlock clicks.
scenes.narration: Think of the exam cupboard. Not everyone gets a key. You lock it after every use. And when old papers aren’t needed any more, you shred them. Pupils’ data deserves the same care.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah at her desk with a results sheet. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! I need to send this term’s results to parents. What’s the safest way?

scenes.visual: One phone, one parent, one result card. A noticeboard with numbers instead of names.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops on the one-to-one card.
scenes.narration: Send each parent only their own child’s result. It takes a little longer, but no family sees another child’s marks. If a list must go on a noticeboard, use exam numbers, not names.

scenes.visual: Five small leak pictures: a register photo, a form, an email, a shared link, an open cupboard.
scenes.animation: Each row slides in with a soft drip sound.
scenes.narration: Look at how data really leaks from schools. A register photographed and posted for a celebration. A form asking for religion when nobody needs it. Pupils’ phone numbers in a teacher’s personal email. A file shared with anyone who has the link. Old records in a cupboard with no lock.

scenes.visual: Four numbered habits on a clean card.
scenes.animation: Steps tick in one by one.
scenes.narration: Small habits fix most of it. Share files with named people only. Use initials or numbers when names aren’t needed. Lock your phone, and lock the cupboard. Delete or shred what you no longer need.

scenes.visual: One key opens three doors: email, files, pupils’ records. Then a shield closes them.
scenes.narration: In the lab, see what one leaked staff password can open, and how pupils’ records go with it. Then see what a unique password and two-step sign-in save.

scenes.visual: Amina holds a football club sign-up form. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A sign-up form for the football club asks every family for their religion and monthly income. Keep those questions, or remove them?

scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: Remove them: a football club doesn’t need them. Remember: know what’s personal, collect only what you need, keep it safe, and delete it when you’re done.

scenes.visual: Amina’s classroom. A pretend trip form on the board; groups cross out questions.
scenes.animation: Lines strike through questions on the board.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: write a pretend trip form with ten questions on the board. Groups cross out every question the trip doesn’t need, and explain why.

checkpoints.prompt: You need to send this term’s results to parents. What’s the safest way?

options.text: Post the full list in the parents’ group
Send each parent only their own child’s result
Pin the full list on the school gate

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — each family sees only their own child’s marks.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a full list shows every child’s marks to everyone. Send each parent only their own child’s result.

checkpoints.prompt: A football club sign-up form asks every family for their religion and monthly income. Keep those questions, or remove them?

options.text: Keep them — more data might be useful later
Remove them — the club doesn’t need them

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — collect only what you need, for a clear reason.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — data you don’t need is only a risk. Remove the questions the club doesn’t need.
